papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
papers.summary:
Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement.
Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities.
We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates.
When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter.
By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter.
The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later.
Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems.
We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections.
Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training.
Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
highlights: Don't Forget What You Just Learned

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: LeafSkill: Efficient Leaf-Level Action Grounding for Recursive LLM Agents
papers.summary:
Recursive large language model (LLM) agents solve long-horizon tasks through decomposition, execution, and environmental feedback.
Yet after producing an atomic subtask, they often invoke the same large model again to translate a familiar instruction into an executable action.
We observe that high-level planning is task-specific, whereas leaf-level action grounding recurs across tasks and can be checked against environment-admitted actions.
We introduce LeafSkill, an external reuse layer that retrieves semantically related grounding experience, binds action templates to current objects and admissible actions, and uses a lightweight 1.7B selector to choose a bound action or defer the unchanged subtask to the original agent.
Skills remain outside the model parameters, allowing a frozen selector to use post-training additions.
Under lexical and syntactic paraphrases, exact matching retrieves none of the reference actions, while semantic retrieval preserves 96.0% and 97.0% candidate coverage; the frozen selector adopts 97.34% of unseen skill types.
On an independent confirmation set of 200 Robotouille tasks, LeafSkill completes 137 tasks versus 121 for ReCAP (68.5% vs.
60.5%, exact McNemar p=.0259).
On the 106 tasks completed by both, it reduces Qwen3.5-27B tokens by 14.42% and calls by 14.08%.
A separate held-out repeat yields a consistent 9.0-point success gain and 18.98% token reduction.
Reusable leaf grounding can thus improve task completion while reducing host-model inference without replacing high-level planning.
highlights: Recursive large language model (LLM) agents solve long-horizon tasks through decomposition, execution, and environmental

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: POSEIDON: Scaling Training Environments for Scientific Agents from Code Repositories
papers.summary:
Training environments remain a major bottleneck for agents in data-driven scientific discovery.
Existing collections of executable and verifiable training environments are small, and their construction remains difficult to scale.
To address this limitation, we introduce Poseidon, an automated pipeline for generating diverse, verifiable training environments from scientific code repositories at scale.
From the same repository budget, Poseidon extracts nearly 10 times as many training environments as a prior approach by decomposing scientific workflows into four complementary task types: Reproduction, Subflow, Completion, and Correction, where each type targets a distinct capability for scientific research.
A recursive improvement loop further refines failed candidates and recovers otherwise discarded environments.
Using Poseidon, we construct Pearl, a collection of 97,659 executable and verifiable environments from 7,110 public repositories spanning 10 scientific disciplines.
To the best of our knowledge, Pearl is the largest and most broadly multidisciplinary collection of scientific-agent training environments to date.
Qwen3.5 models (9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B) trained on Pearl achieve consistent gains across six challenging scientific-agent benchmarks.
Overall, the scale and diversity of Pearl offer opportunities for training scientific discovery agents.
highlights: Training environments remain a major bottleneck for agents in data-driven scientific discovery.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: AgentTrace: Execution-Level Fingerprinting of Black-Box LLM Agents
papers.summary:
Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge.
Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation.
We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces.
AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces.
While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors.
By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing.
Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.
highlights: outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: IGG: A Benchmark for Interactive GUI Grounding under Visibility Constraints
papers.summary:
GUI grounding benchmarks ask whether an agent can localize a target that is already visible in a static screenshot.
Real interfaces often violate this assumption: a target may be off-screen, appear only after a state change or hover, remain occluded, or become actionable after a delay.
This leaves the ability to recover target visibility unevaluated.
To measure this reveal step, we introduce Interactive GUI Grounding (IGG), a benchmark in which an agent must first make the target visible through interaction and then click it.
IGG contains 601 tasks across 16 controllable GUI environments and seven visibility-constraint sub-types, with a compact action space of scrolling, moving, dragging, waiting, and clicking.
In our human study, participants achieve 94.6% accuracy, while GPT-5.5 reaches 79.4% and the strongest evaluated open-source VLM reaches only 31.6%.
To identify the source of this gap, we conduct two controlled interventions.
Telling Qwen3-VL which interaction to perform raises its accuracy only from 30.8% to 33.9%, whereas performing the interaction for the model raises it to 81.9%.
The bottleneck is executing the reveal interaction, not recognizing the target once it is exposed.
We further show that this capability is learnable, demonstrating that visibility recovery can be strengthened consistently across model families.
highlights: first make the target visible through interaction and then click it

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
papers.summary:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer.
But does the point at which risk is easiest to detect also offer the most effective control?
We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state.
The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits.
To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration.
Across three distilled reasoning models and three generation seeds, the strongest gains concentrate in a two- to three-token early window; on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the effect falls to approximately zero at the fourth and fifth tokens, even though later states can be more predictive of risk.
This separates risk readability from effective control: intervention timing must be evaluated through its effect on subsequent generation.
On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline.
An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.
highlights: first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search
papers.summary:
Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs.
However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse.
In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD.
LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation.
KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches.
Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p.
that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%.
Project page and code: https://lems-svd.github.io

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Improving the Energy-Efficiency of the Code Generated by LLMs through Effective Prompting
papers.summary:
As AI-assisted programming becomes increasingly mainstream, the environmental impact of AI-generated software has emerged as an important consideration.
This motivates evaluating LLM-generated code beyond functional correctness by considering execution efficiency and energy consumption.
However, despite substantial advances in code generation, frontier LLMs are rarely evaluated based on the energy efficiency of the code they produce.
In this work, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 21 prompting strategies for energy-efficient code generation and identify 8 strategies for evaluation across 10 widely used open-weight and proprietary LLMs.
We evaluate their effectiveness for both Python and C++ code generation relative to a baseline prompt.
Across the evaluated models, the selected prompting strategies achieved energy reductions of up to 25% for Python and 17% for C++ code generation.
At the model level, Python energy reductions reached up to 50% for Granite-4.0-H-Small, 39% for Claude 4.5 Haiku, and 28% for MiniMax M3, while C++ reductions reached up to 57% for Granite-4.0-H-Small and 6.4% for Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct.
These results demonstrate that prompting strategies can substantially influence the energy consumption of LLM-generated code, although their effectiveness varies across models and programming languages.
Our findings highlight the importance of incorporating energy efficiency into the evaluation and optimization of LLM-based code generation and provide practical insights into designing prompts for more sustainable AI-assisted programming.
highlights: This motivates evaluating LLM-generated code beyond functional correctness by considering execution efficiency and energ

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
papers.summary:
Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct.
We saw this happen in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users.
Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces.
We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release.
We studied whether these formatters misled agents and verifiers and how much the repaired wording helps.
We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with the key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated.
That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted.
Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types.
In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times.
A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness.
We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects.
When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued.
When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best-known open-source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both.
We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged.
Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.
highlights: Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces.
We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Efficient Exploration for Iterative Nash Preference Optimization
papers.summary:
Preference alignment is central to improving large language models (LLMs), but reward-based formulations can be restrictive when human preferences are non-transitive.
Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF) addresses this limitation by modeling alignment as a preference game and seeking a Nash equilibrium.
However, the learning-theoretic foundations of scalable NLHF remain limited: existing regret guarantees rely on explicit preference-model estimation and minimax oracles, whereas simpler iterative methods lack such guarantees.
We study online iterative NLHF and identify exploration as a key obstacle.
First, we show that standard iterative NLHF can incur an exponential dependence on the inverse KL-regularization parameter, demonstrating that implicit exploration through policy updates can be insufficient.
We then propose Exploratory Nash Preference Optimization (ENPO), which combines a SFT-type regularization with adversarial policy exploration.
ENPO eliminates this exponential dependence without requiring minimax oracles or explicit preference-model estimation.
We further introduce Bonus-Explorer ENPO (BENPO), which uses additional oracles to achieve an $O(\log T)$ regret bound.
Finally, we develop Direct ENPO (DENPO), a practical variant of ENPO for fine-tuning LLMs.
Experiments with Llama-3-8B-Instruct demonstrate consistent improvements over the evaluated RLHF and NLHF baselines across multiple benchmarks.
highlights: Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF) addresses this limitation by modeling alignment as a preference game and seekin
We study online iterative NLHF and identify exploration as a key obstacle.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation
papers.summary:
Complex text-to-image requests remain difficult to satisfy reliably. 复杂的文本到图像请求仍然难以可靠地满足。
Verifying and repairing an image can fix an individual output, but a successful repair does not necessarily carry over to other requests. 验证和修复映像可以修复单个输出，但成功的修复不一定会延续到其他请求。
We present ImageRSI, a framework that keeps the image generator frozen and combines three components: five-dimensional verification and repair within each task, an experience library shared across tasks, and offline updating of the judge. 我们提出了ImageRSI ，这是一个保持图像生成器冻结的框架，并结合了三个组成部分：每个任务内的五维验证和修复，跨任务共享的体验库以及法官的离线更新。
Candidate experiences enter the library only after paired A/B validation, and the judge is updated with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on accumulated image-judgment records and evaluated before reuse. 候选人体验只有在配对A/B验证后才能进入库，法官将根据累积的图像判断记录进行有监督的微调和GRPO更新，并在重复使用前进行评估。
We also introduce ImageReq-Bench, a benchmark of 961 requests built around hard cases in real-world image-generation requests, each paired with an evaluation checklist. 我们还介绍了ImageReq-Bench ，这是围绕真实世界图像生成请求中的硬件案例构建的961个请求的基准，每个请求都与评估清单配对。
ImageRSI achieves a Checklist Strict Accuracy (CSA) of 52.6% on MindBench (with Nano Banana Pro as the generator) and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and we compare system outcomes across judge-training configurations. ImageRSI在MindBench （使用Nano Banana Pro作为生成器）上实现了52.6%的Checklist Strict Accuracy （ CSA ） ，在ImageReq-Bench上实现了65.66%的Checklist Strict Accuracy （ CSA ） ，我们比较了不同法官培训配置的系统结果。
highlights: Complex text-to-image requests remain difficult to satisfy reliably.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: PlaceReasoner-Beta: Reasoning-Driven Macro Placement and Benchmarking
papers.summary:
Automated macro placement remains a fundamental challenge in VLSI physical design. 自动化宏观放置仍然是VLSI物理设计中的一个基本挑战。
Despite decades of research, existing approaches predominantly optimize hand-crafted proxy objectives, such as estimated wirelength, and typically produce placements through one-shot numerical optimization, limiting their ability to incorporate visual layout context, codified design expertise, and downstream physical-design feedback in a unified loop. 尽管有数十年的研究，现有的方法主要是优化手工制作的代理目标，例如估计的线长，并且通常通过一次性的数值优化来产生布局，从而限制了它们在统一循环中整合视觉布局背景、编纂设计专业知识和下游物理设计反馈的能力。
We present PlaceReasoner-Beta, a verifier-guided multi-agent framework that reformulates macro placement as a closed-loop reasoning problem rather than black-box optimization. 我们提出了PlaceReasoner-Beta ，这是一个验证者引导的多智能体框架，它将宏观放置重新表述为一个闭环推理问题，而不是黑盒优化。
A vision-language model (VLM) planner generates candidate placements from the floorplan image, macro specifications, and connectivity structure; a geometric verifier enforces physical legality and expert placement principles; a physical verifier refines candidates using early implementation feedback; and a post-route optimizer further improves promising layouts using final PPA. 视觉语言模型（ VLM ）规划器根据平面图图像、宏规范和连接结构生成候选布局；几何验证器执行物理合法性和专家布局原则；物理验证器使用早期实施反馈优化候选；路线后优化器使用最终PPA进一步改进有希望的布局。
To enable reproducible evaluation, we introduce PlaceReasoner-Bench, a fully open end-to-end benchmark built from open RTL designs, EDA tools, and technology libraries. 为了实现可重现的评估，我们引入了PlaceReasoner-Bench ，这是一个完全开放的端到端基准，由开放的RTL设计、EDA工具和技术库构建而成。
It comprises 8 designs at two aspect ratios, yielding 16 tasks with fixed floorplans and I/O assignments, so methods differ only in macro positions and orientations and are evaluated using routed PPA and DRC rather than pre-route proxies.
Across the benchmark, PlaceReasoner-Beta achieves the best timing among DRC-clean methods on all square tasks, reducing post-route TNS by 61.2% at 1:1 and 53.0% at 2:1 relative to the classical baseline field.
It also shortens routed wirelength on most designs despite never explicitly optimizing it, demonstrating that reasoning over spatial structure under physical-design feedback can improve end-to-end layout quality beyond proxy-objective optimization.
highlights: Automated macro placement remains a fundamental challenge in VLSI physical design.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: GaP: A Graph-as-Policy Multi-Agent Self-Learning Harness For Variational Automation Tasks
papers.summary:
For robots to work reliably in commercial and industrial applications, recent advances in agentic coding systems have potential to combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model-free policies.
We focus on "Variational Automation" (VA), a class of tasks that have larger variations in object geometry and pose than fixed automation.
Model-free policies often struggle to close the reliability gap for VA tasks, which must be executed persistently and reliably in commercial and industrial applications.
Motivated by prior work on Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and the Robot Operating System (ROS), we introduce Graph-as-Policy (GaP), a multi-agent coding harness that generates directed computation graphs with perception, planning, and control nodes from a Modular Open Robot Skill Library (MORSL).
GaP generates an internal simulation environment to rehearse task instances with different graphs in parallel to iteratively refine the graph structure and parameters to improve success rates and throughput.
Evaluation with 8 new open VA task benchmarks, 4 in simulation and 4 in real-world, suggests that GaP can achieve success rates that significantly outperform baselines.
Details, code, and data: https://graph-robots.github.io/gap

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
papers.summary:
LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation.
However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses.
To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification.
We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness.
We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability.
In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level.
Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion.
TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Under the Influence: Evaluating and Improving LLM Vigilance in Agentic Tasks
papers.summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly autonomous assistants, capable of accomplishing series of complex tasks by interacting with open world domains such as software databases and the internet.
This presents great opportunity but also great risk: open domains routinely present opportunities for autonomous agents to be influenced by others, e.g.
deciding whether to accept pull requests or whether to use advice on a message board in order to accomplish a task.
Critically, agents must be capable of deciphering when to incorporate benevolent advice into their reasoning, and when to reject malicious advice.
This involves the social capacity of vigilance: the ability to determine which information to use, and which to discard, for effective communication.
While well-studied in humans, the extent to which LLM agents exhibit vigilance is relatively unknown.
Here, we examine LLM agent vigilance in three realistic tasks: navigating dangerous websites, avoiding e-commerce scams, and patching an unsafe code repository.
We find that all frontier models are highly susceptible to malicious influence across all environments.
We also find that model performance itself is surprisingly dissociable from vigilance.
In light of these results, we propose a vigilance harness which uses Bayesian reasoning over a model's estimates of the value of an advisor's advice to decide whether to act on that advice.
The vigilance harness helps recover baseline performance while retaining the benefit of positive influence on agents, paving the way for safer agentic AI systems.
highlights: propose a vigilance harness which uses Bayesian reasoning over a model

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Agentic Hazard Mapper: Emulating Expert Map-Making with AI Agents for Risk Communication
papers.summary:
Hazard maps are essential tools for public risk communication, preparedness, and evacuation planning, yet effective cartographic design is not always ensured due to limited access to cartographic expertise across local governments and communities.
We present Agentic Hazard Mapper, a multi-agent system that automates hazard-map production by emulating professional cartographic workflows and iterative design trade-offs while adapting design decisions to different data, locations, and hazard contexts.
We conducted a formative study with map experts to inform the system design, followed by a user study and interviews with map experts and hazard practitioners.
The generated maps improved participants' spatial understanding and evacuation-planning performance, reduced perceived workload and task completion time, and were generally preferred over corresponding municipal maps.
We further discuss human oversight, adaptation across users and communication contexts, and opportunities to extend agentic support across broader stages of hazard-map production and risk communication.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: OpenStripe supports open-set identification and spatial stripe profiling in wild Amur tigers
papers.summary:
Non-invasive camera-trap monitoring of endangered wildlife requires open-set individual identification---grouping field images into identities without predefined classes or a known population size---yet pose deformation and cluttered backgrounds complicate image comparison.
Here, we present OpenStripe, a multi-agent framework that reconstructs canonical two-dimensional (2D) tiger torso patterns and encodes four interpretable local stripe structures: breakpoints, bifurcations, irregular structures, and round structures.
We evaluated OpenStripe on 100 camera-trap records from 28 wild Amur tigers (Panthera tigris altaica), representing nearly one-third of the documented population in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park.
Combining all four complementary structures enabled automatic identity grouping with 0.90 matched accuracy and a 0.85 adjusted Rand index (ARI), outperforming 49 baseline configurations under the same backend (up to 0.43 accuracy and 0.14 ARI).
In addition, results from OpenStripe indicate that stripe similarity in Amur tigers declines with geographic distance and suggest that traits such as fractal dimension and inter-stripe spacing are associated with geographic proximity.
OpenStripe thus provides an interpretable representation that connects automated individual grouping with spatial phenotypic profiling in wild populations.
highlights: outperforming 49 baseline configurations under the same backend (up to 0

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Same Context, Different Agents: A Behavioral Study of Semantic Layers, Multi-Agent Orchestration and Memory Compaction in Data Agents
papers.summary:
Answering questions over heterogeneous data means combining evidence from files, databases, documents and the web.
Data agents automate this, but their success depends on context.
Three context-engineering techniques (CETs) help by shaping it: semantic layers describe the data, orchestration splits work among agents, and compaction condenses interaction history.
Existing studies validate each CET alone, leaving open how agent behavior shapes its effect.
We present a comprehensive analysis of the three CETs, alone and combined, with seven large language models (LLMs) on 1,514 long-horizon tasks from five benchmarks, covering behavior, accuracy and cost.
We find that data agents without CETs form three behavior groups: investigators, premature answerers that answer without inspecting data, and early stoppers that give up.
Each CET delivers its known benefit, from more investigation to smaller prompts, but only the behavior group it matches turns that benefit into accuracy, such as premature answerers under orchestration.
For investigators, the same CETs can hurt: the semantic layer stops them from looking, orchestration makes them overconfident, costing 5 percentage points, and compaction makes them repeat steps.
Combining CETs yields smaller gains and losses than their sum.
We derive guidance for choosing CETs by agent behavior, task demands and accuracy-cost trade-offs.
highlights: Answering questions over heterogeneous data means combining evidence from files, databases, documents and the web.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification
papers.summary:
The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual.
Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched.
We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap.
BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories.
Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.
highlights: We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Flow-ERD: Agent-type Aware Flow Matching With Entropy-Regularized Distillation for Diverse Traffic Simulation
papers.summary:
Realistic and diverse traffic simulation is essential to autonomous driving development.
Yet prevailing benchmarks predominantly reward realism, and recent methods have optimized accordingly, leaving diversity underexplored.
We introduce Flow-ERD, a multi-agent simulator that pursues realism and diversity jointly.
Its backbone, Agent-Type Aware Flow Matching (AFM), couples flow matching's multi-modal expressiveness with type-specific kinematic execution.
It preserves fine-grained diversity while keeping motions consistent with each agent type.
A second stage, Entropy-Regularized Distillation (ERD), fine-tunes the closed-loop rollout distribution with an entropy-regularized reverse-KL objective.
This mitigates closed-loop covariate shift while explicitly preventing collapse onto high-density modes.
We evaluate Flow-ERD with Cross-Pair Diversity and its validity-gated variant alongside standard realism scores.
Validation experiments further show that tuning entropy regularization recovers most of the pretrained backbone's diversity while retaining realism gains.
Flow-ERD ranks first in test-split realism on the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC) and dominates the validation realism--diversity Pareto front among reproducible baselines.
highlights: first in test-split realism on the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC) and dominates the validation realism--diversi

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Model-Adaptive Tool Necessity Reveals the Knowing-Doing Gap in LLM Tool Use
papers.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as autonomous agents that must decide when to answer directly vs.
when to invoke external tools.
Prior work studying adaptive tool use has largely treated tool necessity as a model-agnostic property, annotated by human or LLM judge, and mostly cover cases where the answer is obvious (e.g., fetching the weather vs.
paraphrasing text).
However, tool necessity in the wild is more nuanced due to the divergence of capability boundaries across models: a problem solvable by a strong model on its own may still require tools for a weaker one.
In this work, we introduce a model-adaptive definition of tool-necessity, grounded in each model's empirical performance.
Following this definition, we compare the necessity against observed tool-call behavior across four models on arithmetic and factual QA dataset, and find substantial mismatches of 26.5-54.0% and 30.8-41.8%, respectively.
To diagnose the failure, we decompose tool use into two stages: an internal cognition stage that reflects whether a model believes a tool is necessary, and an execution stage that determines whether the model actually makes a tool-call action.
By probing the LLM hidden states, we find that both signals are often linearly decodable, yet their probe directions become nearly orthogonal in the late-layer, last-token regime that drives the next-token action.
By tracing the trajectory of samples in the two-stage process, we further discover that the majority of mismatch is concentrated in the cognition-to-action transition, not in cognition itself.
These results reveal a knowing-doing gap in LLM tool-use: improving tool-use reliability requires not only better recognition of when tools are needed, but also better translation of that recognition into action.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: DeepSafe-SciHazard: A Benchmark for Measuring Scientific Safety Risks with Decomposed Harm Scoring
papers.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support science, but they can also convert hazardous scientific knowledge into actionable misuse guidance.
Existing benchmarks often rely on templated queries disconnected from real-world hazards, and employ LLM-as-a-Judge paradigms without domain grounding.
To address this, we introduce SciHazard, a real-world-grounded benchmark for scientific risks and a dataset agnostic evaluation framework for measuring harmfulness.
SciHazard contains 2400 hazardous questions and 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines, with both queries grounded in regulated entities and documented failure scenarios.
To compute \textsc{DeHarm-Score} , we develop a decomposed evaluating procedure that combines query hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk.
For non-refused responses, it further decomposes response-level harm into \textsc{Executability}, quantified via dynamic checklists with importance weighting, and \textsc{Net-new risk}, assessed through retrieval-augmented claim extraction and synthesis-barrier verification.
An expert-validation study shows that \textsc{DeHarm-Score} improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17\% over the strongest baseline.
We benchmark 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents in an extensive scientific safety evaluation.
Notably, deep research agents yield 32.3\% higher mean \textsc{DeHarm-Score} than standard LLMs, exposing autonomous agents as a critical blind spot in current safety defenses.
Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/DeepSafe-Sci.
highlights: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support science, but they can also convert hazardous scientific knowledge into

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Beyond the Monolithic Scheduler: Lightweight Adaptive Policy Switcher for Process Scheduling Optimization
papers.summary:
Modern operating system process schedulers typically enforce a static, ``one-policy-fits-all'' design, which inevitably compromises performance under the highly dynamic and mixed workloads of contemporary edge systems.
Transitioning to dynamic adaptation faces two fundamental challenges: scenario specific static policies lack robust runtime adaptability, whereas computationally intensive AI-assisted policies introduce unacceptable execution overhead for resource-constrained devices.
To structurally resolve this dilemma, we propose the Lightweight Adaptive Policy Switcher (LAPS), a framework that dynamically switches between predefined expert policies, thus decoupling high frequency context switching from low-frequency policy transitions and amortizing transitional overheads.
To eliminate prohibitive online computations, LAPS pre-resolves all heavy dynamic tradeoffs via an offline preparation phase, constructing a strictly overhead-aware Policy Mapping Table.
During runtime, it executes an agentic Observe-Infer-Switch cycle that limits machine learning inference strictly to workload classification.
Consequently, LAPS executes efficient dynamic adaptation simply by mapping the inferred workload state to optimal expert policies via low-cost table lookups.
Experiments show that LAPS achieves an average performance gain of 8.91% and reduces response latency by up to 91.7% in latency-sensitive tasks over the default Linux scheduler EEVDF.
Our results demonstrate that LAPS outperforms the baseline in a wide range of test cases, offering a practical path toward more responsive and intelligent operating systems.
Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/lvmiao233/LAPS.
highlights: outperforms the baseline in a wide range of test cases

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: ToolRACER: A Robust Agentic Conversation Emulation Resource for Agent Training and Evaluation
papers.summary:
Task-oriented conversational agents remain fragile under real world conversation scenarios as they rarely follow a predictable script, especially when users exhibit non-cooperative behavior.
Existing function-calling benchmarks often emphasize successful, cooperative interactions and underrepresent adversarial conversation trajectories, thereby limiting the training resources available for developing robust agents.
We present ToolRACER, a synthetic data generation pipeline that coordinates user, assistant and tool emulation models to generate and validated multi-turn interactions between a user and an agent.
Using ToolRACER, we construct ToolRACERBench a robust multi-turn conversation benchmark spanning six domains, ranging over 55 varied personas, generating a validated corpus of 5.6K conversation trajectories, with approximately 66\% of conversations containing failure-prone conversation scenarios.
We inject adversarial behaviors, producing validated conversational interaction trajectories that capture realistic, robust scenarios.
We evaluate models trained on ToolRACERBench against internal benchmarks, as well as on function calling benchmarks such as $\tau^2$-bench, BFCLv3 and ACEBench to evaluate agentic accuracy and robustness.
Models trained on ToolRACERBench improve end to end agentic accuracy across $\tau^2$-bench and ACEBench, demonstrating significant gains when mixed with in-domain dataset in small language models for agent capability tasks.
highlights: We inject adversarial behaviors, producing validated conversational interaction trajectories that capture realistic, rob

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary:
We introduce Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning (HACRL), a new Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Reward (RLVR) problem that addresses the inefficiencies of isolated multi-agent on-policy optimization.
HACRL enables collaborative optimization with independent execution: heterogeneous agents share verified rollouts during training to mutually improve, while operating independently at inference time.
Unlike LLM-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), HACRL does not require coordinated deployment, and unlike on-/off-policy distillation, it enables bidirectional mutual learning among heterogeneous agents rather than one-directional homogeneous teacher-to-student transfer.
Building on this problem, we propose HACPO, a collaborative RL algorithm that enables principled rollout sharing to maximize sample utilization and cross-agent knowledge transfer.
To mitigate capability discrepancies and policy distribution shifts, HACPO introduces four tailored mechanisms with theoretical guarantees on unbiased advantage estimation.
Extensive experiments across diverse heterogeneous model combinations and reasoning benchmarks show that HACPO consistently improves all participating agents, outperforming GSPO with double rollouts by an average of 3.6% while using only half the rollout cost.
highlights: outperforming GSPO with double rollouts by an average of 3

papers.title: PCFBench: How Far Can Large Vision-Language Models Go in Physics-aware Photonic Inverse Design?
papers.summary:
Photonic crystal fibers (PCFs) underpin critical applications in telecommunications, sensing, and high-power laser delivery, yet their design remains a manual, expert-intensive process that couples geometric intuition with deep waveguide physics.
Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising path toward automating PCF design, but can they truly reason about photonic physics from microscopy images, or do they merely recognize visual patterns?
We introduce PCFBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception, reasoning, and decision steps of the photonic inverse-design loop.
PCFBench spans 26 tasks organized into six categories of increasing cognitive demand (Geometry Perception, Physics Understanding, Text Generation, Multi-modal Reasoning, Inverse-Design Decision, and Code Generation), built from over 220K FDTD simulation samples across 18 structurally diverse fiber families.
We evaluate both individual VLMs on isolated tasks and multi-agent systems (MAS) on the full sequential pipeline from perception to design.
Our results reveal a striking perception-design gap: current models can identify fiber geometry with moderate success, yet consistently fail to translate that visual understanding into physics-aware design actions.
Moreover, cascading agents through the pipeline exposes significant error propagation, where upstream perception mistakes compound into downstream design failures.
These findings suggest that neither model scaling nor naive agent chaining suffices, and that closing the loop demands explicit physical grounding.
PCFBench provides the community with a rigorous, multi-dimensional testbed to measure progress toward AI-assisted photonic engineering.
The project is available at https://pcfbench.github.io/.
highlights: first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs on the perception

papers.title: Permission to Retry: A Study of Authorization and Recovery in AI Agent Workflows
papers.summary:
A durable agent can resume a consequential action while its authority changes and the action's external outcome remains uncertain.
We study execution-time reliability of tool-using AI agents, isolating recovery decisions from language-model behavior.
Checkpoint state, permission to dispatch, evidence of an external effect and permission to reconcile are distinct obligations.
We present a finite conformance study that checks these obligations through histories scored against a provider effect ledger hidden from the recovering application.
A prospectively frozen campaign executes 336 histories on native LangGraph and Temporal hosts, crossing 14 schedules, three provider contracts and four matched application policies.
All 168 paired host cells have identical checked outcomes.
Per host, retained-ledger reconciliation passes all 42 histories: 21 checked completions, 15 denials and six unknown outcomes with reservations retained.
Cached retry, revalidation before retry and stable-key retry pass 30, 36 and 31 histories respectively.
A separate 16-case component study of InfinityOS, an enterprise AI platform developed by Arya.ai, exercises exported authority, worker, recovery and settlement code over repository fakes.
The results isolate the roles of current authority, provider contracts and retained observations in recovery, with safety, completion and unresolved obligations reported separately for the declared application profile.

papers.title: Minimum Description Length Unsupervisedly Separates Law-Grade from Statistical-Grade Knowledge in a Self-Improving Science Agent - and Reveals 86% of Its Own Discoveries Are Statistical
papers.summary:
AI systems that discover scientific relations now generate candidate "laws" at scale, but the bottleneck has shifted from generation to vetting: which candidates deserve belief?
We show that a deployed self-improving science agent - one that has admitted 252 relations through held-out prediction courts - already computes the quantity that answers this question: the Minimum Description Length compression ratio used for model selection doubles, when read under discrete accounting, as an unsupervised epistemic grader.
The compression-ranked top band of the agent's ledger recovers exactly the canonical laws among its discoveries (vis-viva across seven planets, Balmer/Rydberg) plus cross-measurement identities - enrichment $p=3.6\times10^{-12}$ under a hypergeometric test - with zero counterexamples and physically coherent band structure.
The same lens retroactively reveals that 86% of the ledger compresses nothing ($\mathrm{cr}\approx 1$): the agent had been recording statistical regularities, including a learned predictor with held-out $R^2=0.541$ admitted through the prediction gate, under a narrative of compression as the unified value of knowledge - a narrative that was never true for them.
We formalize the resulting dual-axis bookkeeping - prediction value ($R^2$) and compression value (cr) as nearly decoupled axes of knowledge - demonstrate its robustness to quantization, and register forward falsifiable predictions.
The episode is, to our knowledge, the first measured instance of a discovery agent auditing its own knowledge ledger by an internal measure and finding itself over-claiming.
highlights: first measured instance of a discovery agent auditing its own knowledge ledger by an internal measure and finding itself

papers.title: Mining the Design Space of Multi-Agent Workflows
papers.summary:
Designing large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems (MAS) still relies on trial and error and informal "folk wisdom." Manual studies test only a few communication structures or topologies (e.g., sequential, parallel, shared-memory, or debate), while automated optimizers discard search trajectories after selecting a task-specific workflow.
We present a two-phase pipeline for mining reproducible design principles from workflow code and execution traces.
We repurpose AFlow's MCTS optimizer across six composable operators and 26 deterministically verified Enigmata tasks, retaining all intermediate rounds to build a corpus of 28,568 executable workflows.
A sandboxed AutoResearch loop then mines orchestration code and prompt templates under an $L_0$-penalized validation objective and tests candidate principles on held-out searches.
Across 300 feature-mining trials, we identify effects that persist on held-out searches across three levels of workflow design: workflows beginning with independent solvers and one-shot aggregation (Star-first) perform worse ($\Delta = -0.045$); persistent shared documents (SharedMemory) outperform debate ($\Delta = +0.135$); and prompt specificity and placeholder-based context routing yield gains comparable to communication-structure selection ($\Delta = +0.118$).
More broadly, our pipeline and results show the feasibility of turning discarded search trajectories into a statistical testbed for discovering and validating multi-agent workflow design principles.

papers.title: Can AI Agents Help Robotic Engineers? Lessons from Two Focus Days in Industry
papers.summary:
Software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step programming tasks on their own.
However, it is unclear if and how this transfers to robotic engineering, where engineers program industrial robots in niche, vendor-specific languages and rely on visual feedback from simulation tools.
Within this paper, we report a case study on the use of AI agents by an SME that programs industrial robots.
Our results show that the agent did not make the engineers more productive, with the exception of a task that required the generation of highly repetitive code.
However, the results with the agent improved over time, as the engineers learned how to use it and the agent was adapted to the domain.
Moreover, the experience with AI mattered more for the success with the agent than the experience with robotic engineering.
This shows that AI agents are not a plug-and-play solution.
Instead, companies must train their engineers on the usage of agents, plan time for a learning curve, and ensure that agent configurations match the domain and developer requirements.
The strong learning curve we observed further implies that studies on productivity gains with AI should be longitudinal, as they otherwise miss how engineers adopt agents in practice.
highlights: Software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step programming tasks on their own.
Within this paper, we report a case study on the use of AI agents by an SME that programs industrial robots.

papers.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary:
Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance.
We propose NeuroMAS, a method that first treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with LLM agents as nodes and intermediate textual signals as edges.
In NeuroMAS, agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology only determines how information can flow in general, while reinforcement learning training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate.
This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability.
Further, we provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular textual computation is more parameter-efficient when tasks admit hierarchical decompositions.
Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves significantly over both inference-time and trained multi-agent baselines.
We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can be challenging to train from scratch, but become feasible when grown progressively from smaller trained systems.
These results suggest that learned neural multi-agent systems are a promising scaling axis for LLMs.
highlights: first treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with LLM agents

featuredPapers.title: Training Small Language Models for Transferable Tool Selection
featuredPapers.authors: Zhaoyi Zhou, Akshayaa Magesh, Jeongyeol Kwon
featuredPapers.summary:
As LLM agents operate over corpora of more than ten thousand tools, selecting the right tool for a complex multi-step user instruction becomes a central bottleneck.
Tool descriptions cannot all fit in context, and relevance-based retrievers only rank tools without knowing which are actually needed.
Recent work instead leverages proprietary commercial LLMs like Claude or ChatGPT to drive a retriever, decomposing the instruction and selecting over retrieved candidates.
We show that a small, open model can be trained via reinforcement learning to perform the same functionality.
On ToolBench, a Qwen3-8B model post-trained with our recipe outperforms Llama-4-Maverick (402B).
In addition, the trained model transfers directly to different retrievers and generalizes to new tool corpora in different domains.

featuredPapers.title: Same Luck, Different Choice: Twin-World Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
featuredPapers.authors: Zeropy Surio, Tobias Engel, Mei-Lin Chou
featuredPapers.summary:
Agentic reinforcement learning rewards a complete episode, yet the policy needs credit for every decision inside it.
Counterfactual branching estimates this credit by re-running the episode after an alternative decision, but the branch draws its sampling noise independently of the factual episode, so the outcome difference mixes the effect of the decision with the luck of everything that follows.
We observe that in agentic search the retriever, the corpus, and the grader are deterministic, so an episode is a deterministic function of the policy's decisions and its sampling noise.
Twin worlds are therefore realizable: the same noise, a different decision.
We introduce TWICE (TWIn-world Credit Estimation), which keys the Gumbel noise of every token by turn and line, rolls out counterfactual twins that inherit the factual episode's downstream noise, and turns their paired outcome differences into turn-level advantages for policy-gradient updates on actor-sampled trajectories; only the actor is deployed.
Twin credit is unbiased for any coupling quality, its variance is that of an independent counterfactual scaled by $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the twins' outcome correlation, and under coupling the number of rollouts needed to resolve an advantage of size $\Delta$ falls from $\Theta(\Delta^{-2})$ to $\Theta(\Delta^{-1})$.
A square-root rule spends the twin budget where outcomes are predicted to disagree per unit cost.
On seven question-answering benchmarks, TWICE improves the average exact match of GRPO by 5.3 and 4.5 points on Qwen2.5-3B and 7B, outperforms tree-search and counterfactual-branching baselines, and uses 68% fewer auxiliary tokens than VinePPO.

featuredPapers.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
featuredPapers.authors: Jingwei Ni, Dmitry Abulkhanov, Vladislav Smirnov
featuredPapers.summary:
Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one.
Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer.
Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training.
We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control.
It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features.
The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment.
Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy.
The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data.
In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers.
On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.
highlights: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it

featuredPapers.title: Kernel-Managed Shared Memory for System-Wide Personalization
featuredPapers.authors: Ryan Lum, Yongfeng Zhang
featuredPapers.summary:
AI systems become more useful when they can adapt to the people using them, but in multi-agent systems, useful context learned by one agent often remains unavailable to others.
We present kernel-managed shared memory, a system-level abstraction in which specialized agents write structured, tagged memories while the agent-system kernel, not individual agents, governs retrieval, privacy enforcement, and prompt injection.
We implement and evaluate this design on AIOS and compare it against three alternatives across three assistant models (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, Qwen-2.5:7B) and 1,800 total trials.
Against an unmanaged external memory backend (Mem0) using identical underlying storage, kernel-managed retrieval and injection improve personalization scores by 2.4-4.0 points on a 5-point scale (e.g., 1.05 to 4.69 profile usage on GPT-4o), with every comparison significant at p < 10^-18.
Against standard retrieval-augmented injection, gains are similarly large and consistent across all three models.
Against full, unfiltered context concatenation, a soft ceiling on available context rather than on response quality, kernel-managed injection statistically matches performance on two of three models and shows a small, model-specific deficit on the third, while using substantially shorter prompts: end-to-end latency is 15-61% lower across all three models, with corresponding reductions in per-call token usage and inference cost.
These results indicate that centralizing memory management in the agent-system kernel, rather than leaving retrieval and privacy enforcement to individual agents, delivers most of the personalization benefit of unconstrained context at a fraction of its cost.
highlights: Against standard retrieval-augmented injection, gains are similarly large and consistent across all three models.

featuredPapers.title: ADAPT for Science: A Multi-Agent System for Self-Evolving Scientific Optimization
featuredPapers.authors: Zhaoran Feng, Yuchen Ni, Jianan Liu
featuredPapers.summary:
Scientific discovery often requires identifying a small number of high-performing designs in vast, constrained search spaces.
This is difficult when evaluations are costly, feasible solutions are sparse, parameters are strongly coupled, and physical constraints are strict.
Recent AI for AI methods can automatically improve algorithms and optimization procedures.
However, general purpose approaches are not designed around scientific priors, physical constraints, and limited evaluation budgets.
We introduce ADAPT for Science, a multi-agent framework that treats scientific optimization as two coupled decisions: where to search and how to search.
ADAPT uses historical designs to identify promising and diverse initial conditions, progressively concentrates computation on favorable search directions, and evolves the optimization procedure from execution feedback.
We evaluate ADAPT on the design of gravitational wave detectors using a differentiable physics simulator and eight unseen detector topologies.
Under matched scientific evaluation budgets, ADAPT achieves a mean loss of 0.204 +/- 0.101, reducing loss by 54.9% relative to the best classical optimizer and by 62.2% relative to the best general purpose agentic evolution baseline.
ADAPT achieves the lowest loss on all unseen topologies among the evaluated baselines.
ADAPT provides a step toward scientific optimization systems that continuously learn from prior experience and their own search outcomes.

featuredPapers.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
featuredPapers.authors: Ziyi Jiao, Heng Zhang, Drishti Regmi
featuredPapers.summary:
Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget.
We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents.
A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation.
The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories.
These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies.
A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding.
The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure.
A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions.
The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion.
Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.

featuredPapers.title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection via LLM-based Reasoning
featuredPapers.authors: Yiheng Li, Jingyue Li
featuredPapers.summary:
With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat.
Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment.
Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads.
In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL).
Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities.
We constructed a comprehensive evaluation benchmark comprising eight textual and seven visual malicious categories, supplemented with benign datasets to rigorously test for false positives.
Our evaluation across multiple leading LLMs, including Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash, demonstrates the efficacy and generalizability of this approach.
The proposed method achieves up to 90.91% accuracy and 100% recall on textual tasks.
In the visual domain, it achieves up to 99.28% accuracy while maintaining 100% precision across all evaluated models.
Crucially, when evaluated against 500 highly obfuscated environmental web-agent injections (WebInject), MPIDetector achieved a detection rate up to 99.80%.
Comparisons with two baseline approaches for detecting textual PI payloads, along with two additional methods for visual input detection, demonstrate MPIDetector's superior accuracy.
These results show that LLM-driven reasoning provides a robust, cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injections.

featuredPapers.title: R$^2$Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop
featuredPapers.authors: Mingda Zhang, Yun Huang, Qiang Huang
featuredPapers.summary:
In recent years, agentic orchestration has been widely applied to solve complex human tasks.
However, existing orchestration learning still faces key challenges, including hand-designed curricula, advantage collapse when a task's rollouts all reach the same outcome, and unreliable evaluation signals that judge each skill by one noisy score.
To address these challenges, we propose R$^2$Orch, a new paradigm of Recursive Self-Play Orchestration: an inner loop of self-play that improves the orchestrator on self-chosen tasks, and an outer loop that improves how the inner loop improves.
To support this paradigm, we introduce Recursive Learnability, a training objective that rewards a Proposer for choosing tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn.
Built on this objective, we further propose Skill Withdrawal, in which the outer loop withdraws each skill once a controlled evaluation within self-play shows that the orchestrator performs as well without it.
Moreover, the two loops form one cycle: failures are distilled into skills, skills into parameters, and withdrawals lead the Proposer to new failures, so the orchestrator moves toward zero-skill deployment.
Experimental results on twelve datasets show that R$^2$Orch consistently outperforms baselines across question answering, math, code, and interactive tasks.
Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/R2Orch.

featuredPapers.title: CollabFlow: Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Collaboration
featuredPapers.authors: Xiao Huang, Mingda Zhang, Junming Zhang
featuredPapers.summary:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets a system improve from its own outcomes; in LLM-based multi-agent systems, Agents refine one another within a task, and outcomes improve how they collaborate across tasks.
However, existing multi-agent collaboration leaves this loop open: collaboration is pre-defined at the operator level, topology-only learning keeps verbatim exchange that propagates errors, and reward maximization on a system's own outcomes concentrates on a few teams.
To address these challenges, we propose CollabFlow, an RSI system of Learned Agent Collaboration: a trainable Collab-Director constructs teams of complete Agents, a frozen executor runs them, and each round's outcomes retrain the director.
Within each round, the edges of a collaboration graph carry protocols of Evidence-Conditioned Communication: a receiver adopts a differing answer only when the sender's evidence is stronger by a margin, so the director learns who communicates and how.
Across rounds, we further propose Collaborative Trajectory Balance (CTB), a flow-based objective that credits each team once across its construction orders and targets a reward-proportional distribution over teams, so several good teams stay in play.
We also bound how far this self-generated target moves between rounds, which shrinks as records accumulate.
On twelve datasets, CollabFlow outperforms all baselines and keeps improving across rounds.
Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CollabFlow-631E.
highlights: outperforms all baselines and keeps improving across rounds

featuredPapers.title: Building Presentation Intelligence for High-Quality Slide Generation
featuredPapers.authors: Yuhang Xie, Cheng Li, Chenliang Li
featuredPapers.summary:
PowerPoint presentations (PPTs) are a dominant medium for communication across diverse domains, yet high-quality PPT generation still depends heavily on labor-intensive human effort.
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) for agentic tasks have created both new opportunities and challenges (Chen et al., 2026) for automatic PPT generation.
In this work, we present a unified training framework for automatic PPT generation toward presentation intelligence, integrating cross-validated data synthesis, guided teacher enhancement, and verifiable reward optimization.
We first construct a cross-validated pipeline for data synthesis, with explicit control over both difficulty and validity.
We then develop a teacher-enhancement framework grounded in rules and prior knowledge to substantially strengthen the instructional capacity of teacher models.
Building on this, we further improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) through a mixed-teacher strategy and a lightweight outcome-driven trajectory filtering method.
Finally, based on the resulting SFT models, we introduce a suite of verifiable aesthetic metrics together with a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework to optimize slide-level visual attributes beyond text-only supervision.
Experiments show that our enhanced SFT pipeline improves Qwen-3.6-27B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B by 7.45 and 9.35 points on PresentBench, respectively, surpassing GLM-5.2 while maintaining strong generalization.
Reinforcement learning further improves performance across five aesthetic dimensions, compensating for the limitations of SFT in visual refinement.
Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for high-quality PPT generation.

featuredPapers.title: CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU
featuredPapers.authors: Deng Pan, Xue-Jian Gao, Junyi Fan
featuredPapers.summary:
Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate.
Although AI agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs, potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data.
We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and a Self-Evolving Agent.
On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, CAKE's aggregated results achieve $100\%$ case pass rate on the standard set (1,060/1,060) and $98.28\%$ on the hidden set (4,167/4,240), with an overall mean score of 78.63 out of 100 and an average performance speedup of $1.334\times$ over the baseline.
Evolution then pushes correct operators further: EngramGateFusion cuts aggregate device time by $46.6\%$ over 20 rounds and roughly halves the mean roofline gap.
These results offer a practical path toward closing Ascend's AI-for-kernel capability gap.
highlights: These results offer a practical path toward closing Ascend's AI-for-kernel capability gap.

featuredPapers.title: Muffin - A Shared Memory Buffer for Asynchronous AI Agents
featuredPapers.authors: Ping-Lin Kuo, Suman Navaratnarajah, Christian Frey
featuredPapers.summary:
The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection.
However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains.
A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination.
Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework.
In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local.
Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.

featuredPapers.title: R$^2$ Flow: Recursive Self-Improvement via Recursive Skill Evolution
featuredPapers.authors: Mingda Zhang, Qiang Huang, Yanjin Li
featuredPapers.summary:
LLM-based agents can improve themselves across tasks by reusing and revising the skills they orchestrate into executable procedures.
Flow-based training fits this loop: it samples procedures in proportion to reward, and the flow through each skill credits it for the next library revision.
Three obstacles stand in the way of making this self-improvement reliable: flow training suffers strategy collapse over tree-structured histories; nonnegative flow-based credit rewards frequent use as if it were benefit; and library edits rest on the task reward the policy optimizes.
We introduce R$^2$ Flow, a recursive self-improvement framework that alternates policy learning, independent verification, and versioned skill-library updates on a shared-state orchestration graph.
The graph merges histories that differ only in the order of independent steps, allowing flow training to pool evidence across equivalent executions.
A flow-share readout of the trained flow, invariant to the backward policy, and a separate signed utility rank which skills to change, verifier evidence decides whether an edit is warranted, and a residual-variance plateau sets when to update.
Committed edits reshape the graph the next policy learns on, realizing recursive skill evolution.
Across question answering, mathematical reasoning, interactive decision making, and code generation, R$^2$ Flow improves task accuracy and library-edit precision over heuristic orchestration, reinforcement learning, and skill-evolution baselines, and transfers across executors.
Code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/r2flow.
highlights: LLM-based agents can improve themselves across tasks by reusing and revising the skills they orchestrate into executable

featuredPapers.title: RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?
featuredPapers.authors: Kaiwen Zhou, Udari Madhushani Sehwag
featuredPapers.summary:
Recursive self-improvement, in which frontier AI models work on training the next generation, is quickly becoming a reality.
However, the safety of this process has received far less attention than it should.
A misaligned model training its successor can shape what that successor knows, how it behaves, and what it wants, and the harm carries forward into the next generation.
We study this risk through the lens of AI control.
We introduce RSI Control Arena, a testbed in which a frontier model, acting as an autonomous R\&D agent, is given a benign main task from a stage of a successor model's training pipeline together with a covert side task to install a misaligned property in the successor.
The testbed contains 16 side tasks in three classes, forming 22 task pairs with main tasks that span the pipeline from data curation to reinforcement learning.
We evaluate six frontier models as agents against LLM monitors that read the transcript of the run and the agent's reasoning.
We observe that every model completes a substantial share of the side tasks without degrading the main-task performance, including side tasks that make the successor itself a better saboteur.
Under minimal instructions to stay covert, models already produce successful attacks that monitors fail to detect, and providing a short list of evasion tactics further reduces the detection rate.
Monitors with access to agent's reasoning detects most attacks, but not all.
Our results indicate that recursive self-improvement raises significant safety concerns, and that strong safety effort should be in place before models are trusted with greater responsibility of training their successors.

featuredPapers.title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
featuredPapers.authors: Kaijian Zou, Vaibhav Chennareddy, Yunxiang Zhang
featuredPapers.summary:
Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories.
Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs.
Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead.
We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification.
It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution.
We train SWE-Verifier from Qwen3.5-4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric-guided teacher scores.
Using the mini-swe-agent harness, SWE-Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax-M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek-V4-Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost.
Across both models, SWE-Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all-step baselines at substantially lower cost.
These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding-agent performance and inference efficiency.
Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE-Verifier.
highlights: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories.
