featuredPapers.title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
featuredPapers.authors: Fabian Isensee, Constantin Ulrich Harsy, Maximilian Rokuss
featuredPapers.summary:
Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it.
General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code.
We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback.
Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request.
Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it.
On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation.
A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate.
Code: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nninteractive-agent

featuredPapers.title: Harnessing Language Models as Optimization Modeling Agents
featuredPapers.authors: Yunxiang Luo, Xin Xu, Tianhao Chen
featuredPapers.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language optimization problems into solver programs, but reliably producing correct formulations and implementations remains challenging.
Existing approaches improve optimization modeling through agentic workflows or task-specific post-training.
This raises a practical question: can a lightweight harness using a single model role achieve competitive performance without additional training?
We introduce OPTICYCLE and OPTISTATE, two lightweight inference harnesses for optimization modeling, and evaluate them on nine benchmarks comprising 2,634 problems using 11 Qwen variants spanning 0.6B-27B parameters.
Our results show that execution-guided revision consistently improves macro accuracy over direct generation for all evaluated models, with gains of up to 49.46 percentage points.
Despite their simplicity, both harnesses outperform six adapted agentic workflows in same-model comparisons and four evaluated post-trained optimization models at comparable model sizes, without additional training.
Explicit formulation state provides further but model-dependent improvements, suggesting that additional structure is not universally beneficial.

featuredPapers.title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
featuredPapers.authors: Yang Li, Yike Wang, Di Wan
featuredPapers.summary:
Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances and the effects of earlier actions.
We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real-survey data.
Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments.
Trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, sharp-421m-mlx achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 on one-shot consumer financial-choice tasks derived from held-out survey responses.
Its accuracy exceeds GLM-5.3-Flash, Jev 1.13, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GPT-6-Luna and GPT-6-Astra in the common benchmark (full test for the first four; matched 500-group sample for Astra).
We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions.
Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups.
Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age-income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase.
Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt.
A response-stratified 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers.
S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.

featuredPapers.title: A Three-Pillar Governance Framework for Safe and Trustworthy AI Agents
featuredPapers.authors: Edward C. Cheng, Jeshua Cheng, Alice Siu
featuredPapers.summary:
AI agents capable of autonomous decision-making introduce significant challenges related to safety, alignment, accountability, and human oversight.
Existing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and responsible AI approaches provide important foundations, but many remain fragmented across system design, governance, and operational deployment.
This paper presents a Three-Pillar (3P) model and framework for developing safe and trustworthy AI agents through transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness.
The framework defines an evolutionary path in which increasing agent autonomy is introduced through progressive validation, structured human oversight, and auditable operational controls.
We further describe how the model supports agent lifecycle monitoring, decision traceability, escalation management, and human-agent collaboration within enterprise agentic environments.
By integrating oversight principles with operational mechanisms, the proposed framework provides a practical foundation for deploying AI agents that remain aligned with human intent while enabling controlled progression toward higher autonomy.

featuredPapers.title: EvoSteer: Online Self-Evolving Graph Orchestration via Reference-Anchored Credit Assignment
featuredPapers.authors: Mingda Zhang, Hanwen Zhang, Qiang Huang
featuredPapers.summary:
In recent years, LLM-based multi-agent systems have been widely applied to orchestrate tool-using agents into executable communication graphs.
However, existing self-evolving orchestration still faces key challenges, including post-hoc evolution that revises the team only after the trajectory ends, credit diffusion that gives every action the same terminal advantage under confounded baselines, and skill admission that is uncalibrated and never retired.
To address these challenges, we propose EvoSteer, a new paradigm of Online Self-Evolving Graph Orchestration -- the orchestrator builds a running team and repairs its plausible but failing steps from execution features and a learned value estimate.
To support this paradigm, we introduce Anchored Trajectory Balance (AnchorTB), a regression-style flow-matching loss that assigns each orchestration action a coefficient by balancing subtrajectories against a frozen reference.
Built on the learned flow, we further propose Validated Skill Admission, in which a candidate skill is tried before promotion and promoted only if paired evidence passes a sequential test under a shared nominal testing budget.
Moreover, AnchorTB combines measured task-level reference reward statistics with prefix-dependent corrections.
Experimental results on twelve datasets show that EvoSteer significantly outperforms baselines across question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive decision making.
Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/evosteer.

papers.title: Training Small Language Models for Transferable Tool Selection
papers.summary:
As LLM agents operate over corpora of more than ten thousand tools, selecting the right tool for a complex multi-step user instruction becomes a central bottleneck.
Tool descriptions cannot all fit in context, and relevance-based retrievers only rank tools without knowing which are actually needed.
Recent work instead leverages proprietary commercial LLMs like Claude or ChatGPT to drive a retriever, decomposing the instruction and selecting over retrieved candidates.
We show that a small, open model can be trained via reinforcement learning to perform the same functionality.
On ToolBench, a Qwen3-8B model post-trained with our recipe outperforms Llama-4-Maverick (402B).
In addition, the trained model transfers directly to different retrievers and generalizes to new tool corpora in different domains.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Same Luck, Different Choice: Twin-World Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary:
Agentic reinforcement learning rewards a complete episode, yet the policy needs credit for every decision inside it.
Counterfactual branching estimates this credit by re-running the episode after an alternative decision, but the branch draws its sampling noise independently of the factual episode, so the outcome difference mixes the effect of the decision with the luck of everything that follows.
We observe that in agentic search the retriever, the corpus, and the grader are deterministic, so an episode is a deterministic function of the policy's decisions and its sampling noise.
Twin worlds are therefore realizable: the same noise, a different decision.
We introduce TWICE (TWIn-world Credit Estimation), which keys the Gumbel noise of every token by turn and line, rolls out counterfactual twins that inherit the factual episode's downstream noise, and turns their paired outcome differences into turn-level advantages for policy-gradient updates on actor-sampled trajectories; only the actor is deployed.
Twin credit is unbiased for any coupling quality, its variance is that of an independent counterfactual scaled by $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the twins' outcome correlation, and under coupling the number of rollouts needed to resolve an advantage of size $\Delta$ falls from $\Theta(\Delta^{-2})$ to $\Theta(\Delta^{-1})$.
A square-root rule spends the twin budget where outcomes are predicted to disagree per unit cost.
On seven question-answering benchmarks, TWICE improves the average exact match of GRPO by 5.3 and 4.5 points on Qwen2.5-3B and 7B, outperforms tree-search and counterfactual-branching baselines, and uses 68% fewer auxiliary tokens than VinePPO.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
papers.summary:
Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one.
Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer.
Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training.
We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control.
It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features.
The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment.
Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy.
The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data.
In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers.
On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.
highlights: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Kernel-Managed Shared Memory for System-Wide Personalization
papers.summary:
AI systems become more useful when they can adapt to the people using them, but in multi-agent systems, useful context learned by one agent often remains unavailable to others.
We present kernel-managed shared memory, a system-level abstraction in which specialized agents write structured, tagged memories while the agent-system kernel, not individual agents, governs retrieval, privacy enforcement, and prompt injection.
We implement and evaluate this design on AIOS and compare it against three alternatives across three assistant models (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, Qwen-2.5:7B) and 1,800 total trials.
Against an unmanaged external memory backend (Mem0) using identical underlying storage, kernel-managed retrieval and injection improve personalization scores by 2.4-4.0 points on a 5-point scale (e.g., 1.05 to 4.69 profile usage on GPT-4o), with every comparison significant at p < 10^-18.
Against standard retrieval-augmented injection, gains are similarly large and consistent across all three models.
Against full, unfiltered context concatenation, a soft ceiling on available context rather than on response quality, kernel-managed injection statistically matches performance on two of three models and shows a small, model-specific deficit on the third, while using substantially shorter prompts: end-to-end latency is 15-61% lower across all three models, with corresponding reductions in per-call token usage and inference cost.
These results indicate that centralizing memory management in the agent-system kernel, rather than leaving retrieval and privacy enforcement to individual agents, delivers most of the personalization benefit of unconstrained context at a fraction of its cost.
highlights: Against standard retrieval-augmented injection, gains are similarly large and consistent across all three models.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
papers.summary:
Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget.
We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents.
A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation.
The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories.
These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies.
A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding.
The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure.
A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions.
The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion.
Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.
highlights: We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructe

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection via LLM-based Reasoning
papers.summary:
With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat.
Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment.
Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads.
In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL).
Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities.
We constructed a comprehensive evaluation benchmark comprising eight textual and seven visual malicious categories, supplemented with benign datasets to rigorously test for false positives.
Our evaluation across multiple leading LLMs, including Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash, demonstrates the efficacy and generalizability of this approach.
The proposed method achieves up to 90.91% accuracy and 100% recall on textual tasks.
In the visual domain, it achieves up to 99.28% accuracy while maintaining 100% precision across all evaluated models.
Crucially, when evaluated against 500 highly obfuscated environmental web-agent injections (WebInject), MPIDetector achieved a detection rate up to 99.80%.
Comparisons with two baseline approaches for detecting textual PI payloads, along with two additional methods for visual input detection, demonstrate MPIDetector's superior accuracy.
These results show that LLM-driven reasoning provides a robust, cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injections.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Building Presentation Intelligence for High-Quality Slide Generation
papers.summary:
PowerPoint presentations (PPTs) are a dominant medium for communication across diverse domains, yet high-quality PPT generation still depends heavily on labor-intensive human effort.
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) for agentic tasks have created both new opportunities and challenges (Chen et al., 2026) for automatic PPT generation.
In this work, we present a unified training framework for automatic PPT generation toward presentation intelligence, integrating cross-validated data synthesis, guided teacher enhancement, and verifiable reward optimization.
We first construct a cross-validated pipeline for data synthesis, with explicit control over both difficulty and validity.
We then develop a teacher-enhancement framework grounded in rules and prior knowledge to substantially strengthen the instructional capacity of teacher models.
Building on this, we further improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) through a mixed-teacher strategy and a lightweight outcome-driven trajectory filtering method.
Finally, based on the resulting SFT models, we introduce a suite of verifiable aesthetic metrics together with a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework to optimize slide-level visual attributes beyond text-only supervision.
Experiments show that our enhanced SFT pipeline improves Qwen-3.6-27B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B by 7.45 and 9.35 points on PresentBench, respectively, surpassing GLM-5.2 while maintaining strong generalization.
Reinforcement learning further improves performance across five aesthetic dimensions, compensating for the limitations of SFT in visual refinement.
Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for high-quality PPT generation.
highlights: first construct a cross-validated pipeline for data synthesis
