papers.title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary:
Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context.
However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution.
Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory.
Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories.
To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization.
At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation.
At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution.
Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average.
Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.
highlights: outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: ChaosBench-Logic: A Benchmark for Logical and Symbolic Reasoning on Chaotic Dynamical Systems
papers.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language tasks but remain brittle in domains requiring precise logical and symbolic reasoning.
Chaotic dynamical systems provide an especially demanding test because chaos is deterministic yet often misinterpreted as randomness or complexity.
We introduce ChaosBench-Logic, a benchmark that evaluates LLM reasoning across 30 diverse dynamical systems using a unified first-order logic (FOL) ontology.
Each system is annotated with truth assignments for 11 semantic predicates, and 621 questions are generated across seven reasoning categories, including multi-hop implications, cross-system analogies, counterfactual reasoning, bias probes, and multi-turn dialogues.
We define metrics for logical accuracy, implication consistency, dialogue coherence, and contradiction, and we release an open-source evaluation pipeline.
Initial experiments show that frontier LLMs such as GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and the open-source LLaMA-3 70B achieve 91-94% per-item accuracy, yet still score 0% on compositional items and exhibit fragile global coherence.
Dialogue-level accuracy ranges from 53.1% (GPT-4 CoT) to 75.5% (LLaMA-3 zero-shot).
ChaosBench-Logic provides a rigorous testbed for diagnosing such failures and a foundation for developing neuro-symbolic approaches that improve scientific reasoning in LLMs.
highlights: Large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language tasks but remain brittle in domains requiring precise logical and

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation
papers.summary:
Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations.
We introduce IneqAgent, an agentic framework combining LLM reasoning with symbolic computation for inequality proving in Lean4.
Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection.
Complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates for local Lean proof generation.
The agent integrates these proofs with LLM-generated steps and uses Lean feedback to construct complete proofs checked against the original theorem statements.
On four benchmarks, IneqAgent with DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), achieving the highest overall success rate among the evaluated methods.
Across four backbones, it achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than Direct Agent using the same backbone, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs.
We also obtain Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five, and certify the Holens--Djokovic $(4,4)$ inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.
highlights: Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate le

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code
papers.summary:
We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale.
3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding.
First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code.
We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents.
Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records.
Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content.
It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation.
Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models.
Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.
highlights: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content a

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: ISW-Agent: Integrating LLM-Driven Dialogue with n8n Workflow for Internal Solitary Wave Remote Sensing Image Processing
papers.summary:
Internal solitary wave (ISW) remote sensing requires task parameters and spatial information to be transferred across image acquisition, detection, stripe extraction, and propagation prediction.
Here, we present ISW-Agent, which integrates large language model (LLM) interpretation with n8n workflows and independent scientific models through structured task constraints, geospatial transformations, and stage-specific output validation.
In tests of 120 Chinese instructions per backend, GPT-5.6 Sol and DeepSeek both achieved a strict task-match rate of 94.2%, with all intents and execution decisions matching the reference.
Sentinel-1 cases demonstrated continuous processing from dialogue requests to wavefront prediction for the specified scene.
Of 50 timed scenes, 39 completed detection, extraction, and prediction with a median turnaround time of 48.04 s; 11 stopped after empty extraction.
Across 3,408 controlled fault-injection runs, retries recovered 234 transient-failure conditions and output validation rejected 234 structural defects, while 61 provenance or completeness errors indicated the need for content-consistency checks.
Overall, ISW-Agent thus connects natural-language requests to traceable spatial processing chains for multimodel ISW analysis.
highlights: Sentinel-1 cases demonstrated continuous processing from dialogue requests to wavefront prediction for the specified sce

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents
papers.summary:
Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails.
Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed.
The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step.
However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor.
To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent's latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward.
LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent.
Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers.
Specifically, we compare the weak model's hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty.
During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training.
Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55--11.94 points at matched escalation rates.
With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
papers.summary:
Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs).
Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics.
Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries.
We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use.
To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent.
We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy.
Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.
highlights: outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Adapting the Interface, Not the Model: Runtime Harness Adaptation for Deterministic LLM Agents
papers.summary:
LLM agents are shaped not only by their language models, but also by the runtime harness that mediates observation, tool use, action execution, feedback interpretation, and trajectory control.
While existing agent adaptation methods mainly update model parameters, many failures in deterministic, rule-governed domains stem from mismatches at the model--environment interface.
We propose Life-Harness, a lifecycle-aware runtime harness that improves frozen LLM agents without changing model weights or evaluation environments.
Life-Harness evolves from training trajectories by converting recurring interaction failures into reusable interventions across environment contracts, procedural skills, action realization, and trajectory regulation, and remains fixed for evaluation on unseen tasks.
We evaluate Life-Harness across eight environments from AgentBench, $\tau$-bench, $\tau^2$-bench, and AppWorld using 18 open-weight backbones, and further test three frontier models on seven environments.
With Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Life-Harness exceeds Meta-Harness and AHE by 28.7 and 7.5 percentage points in mean accuracy across the seven shared environments, respectively, while using 8.5\% and 68.4\% fewer optimization tokens.
The evolved harnesses also benefit GPT 5.5, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding an average accuracy gain of 3.5 percentage points.
Code is available at https://github.com/Tianshi-Xu/Life-Harness.
highlights: Adapting the Interface, Not the Model

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
papers.summary:
We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon.
Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory.
No one assigned roles or wrote game logic.
The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves.
Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene.
Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way.
To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans.
Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day.
Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination.
We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.
highlights: first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents
We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dr

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Stronger Judges Do Not See More: Deployment-Integrity Blindness in LLM Evaluation
papers.summary:
LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported.
A tampered deployment that preserves evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator.
We introduce DIB-Bench, a benchmark that measures this deployment-integrity blindness across 7,560 scored examples, six tamper types, and an evaluator ladder from regex scorers through LLM judges to GPT-5-nano.
Stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs: mean acceptance rises from 88.6% (rule-based) to 94.1% (GPT-5-nano), and a trigger-conditional tamper invisible on the evaluation suite produces 48-100% harmful outputs, rising with model capability.
A PAC-style bound shows that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size; a manifest-hash identity channel detects them with zero samples.
Behavioral fingerprinting identifies the model component above chance (76.7%) but covers one of six stack components.
We also propose a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.
highlights: Stronger Judges Do Not See More
LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: ContinualSkillBench: Can LLM Agents Truly Evolve Their Capabilities?
papers.summary:
Modern agent frameworks equip large language models with external skill libraries to solve complex tasks.
However, it remains unclear whether these systems can effectively evolve their skills and whether the resulting skills improve task-solving capabilities.
To bridge this gap, we introduce ContinualSkillBench, a dynamic evaluation framework for in-context continual skill learning.
It covers five domains, each with 100 tasks ordered by difficulty and opportunities for skill transfer.
Our experiments show that sequential execution generally improves performance, but the gains vary substantially across models and domains.
Moreover, across two models and three domains, retaining context and feedback without skill maintenance yields nearly the same mean performance as maintaining an explicit skill library.
Explicit skills nevertheless provide selective benefits for tasks requiring reusable procedures or precise outputs.
We further find that the weaker model (GPT-4o) accumulates more skills but reuses them less often, suggesting difficulty consolidating task-specific experience into reusable procedures.
These findings show that current in-context skill evolution mechanisms can support continual adaptation, but still struggle to consistently consolidate experience into robust and transferable skills.
highlights: Modern agent frameworks equip large language models with external skill libraries to solve complex tasks.

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary:
Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents.
However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation.
Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation.
Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget.
This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability.
PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions.
It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline.
We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets.
Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints.
These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.
highlights: first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents
papers.summary:
Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair selection as they grow.
We present TRACER, a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors.
On a mixed retail-and-telecom $\tau^2$ environment, TRACER improves GPT-5.4's tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing input tokens per step by 80%, exposing just 5 of 128 tools.
In autonomous full-turn execution, it matches GPT-5.4's full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step.
Across six environments and four models, TRACER improves tool-selection accuracy over full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs, with average gains of 6 to 10 points; the three exceptions trail by at most 2.2.
We analyze failures in both regimes to identify directions for future work.
highlights: Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair select

papers.groupName: 重点跟进（产业界 / 端云结合）
papers.title: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures
papers.summary:
When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data.
We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed.
We study it in a controlled agent environment, on one failure (asking a clarifying question when the request was already unambiguous), with labels from a rule-based overseer validated against blind human judgment.
Claims cover eligible models, which both over-ask and sometimes act on matched unambiguous requests: five of thirteen qualified (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4).
Four findings.
First, the ask-vs-act decision is causally localizable in every eligible family: a direction learned from intervention labels flips 72-100% of held-out over-asks at a definite residual-stream depth, with site and dose chosen on training data, and random directions under the same procedure flip at most one episode.
Second, over-asking has two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert and orthogonal to the decision) and asks anyway; in the fifth, the rare over-asks track different world-representations.
Third, steering gated on a probe readout removes most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate questions survive (bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero); a prompt instruction makes it worse.
Fourth, consolidating the fix into the weights yields a map, not a rule: on one model a LoRA confined to the causal band passes every criterion fixed in advance while behavior cloning on identical data breaks retention; on three families the reverse holds; on the fifth the outcome crosses the boundary across seeds.
A geometric rule written down in advance to predict the regime failed on two out-of-family tests; we report the failure and stop rather than fit a replacement.
highlights: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Global Coherence: When Every Agent Is Right and the Team Is Still Wrong - A Local-to-Global Semantic Foundation for Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.summary:
AI agents can each make locally valid decisions yet jointly produce an invalid result.
We call this the global coherence problem: a failure of shared state, not merely of intelligence.
Our Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem gives the exact boundary.
A policy can guarantee a valid action exactly when all worlds producing the same observation share an admissible action.
If k indistinguishable worlds require pairwise-disjoint actions, the best randomized worst-case success is 1/k; more reasoning, roles, messages, or samples cannot recover the missing distinction.
A stronger model can reason better within its context, but it cannot see beyond it.
The smallest sufficient context is NP-hard to find, yet counterexample-guided refinement finds a sufficient one and recertifies it as rules change.
We give local-to-global runtime semantics X = (H, C, G, F; D): topology H records overlapping scopes; category C governs state-changing actions; groupoid G keeps reversible translations; sheaf F tests whether local views glue into one world; and history D keeps only what alters legal futures.
Each preserves the needed information as state is split, translated, or changed.
Models propose; the harness owns shared state and governs commit.
Ten studies test the boundary.
On a revision benchmark, a frontier model scores 40/40 when the deciding event is visible; hidden, every arm is consistent with chance (1/3); one restored fact returns 40/40.
On TeamBench, ordinary teams exceed a shared budget in 5/5 runs, a visible live count leaves 4/5, and commit enforcement leaves 0/5.
In tau2-bench Telecom, current-state checks score 0.07 after silent reverts; the harness scores 1.00.
Refinement keeps a sufficient context through rule changes at 28% of the all-field cost.
Solvers that already own the state tie it, as predicted.
Local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state.
highlights: exceed a shared budget in 5/5 runs

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Self-improving data synthesis enables scalable adaptation of embedding models
papers.summary:
AI agents require specialised retrieval across domains and tasks, but adapting embedding models is constrained by costly manual training-data design.
Here we introduce SYNTRA, a self-improving agentic framework that turns a few retrieval examples into reusable synthesis instructions.
Given an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs, SYNTRA infers implicit information needs and relevance criteria, then uses feedback on trial outputs to refine instructions for query generation and relevance assessment.
Experiments across 24 datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate that the same synthesis workflow produces effective training data, benefiting even strong embedding models with and without existing labelled training sets.
Self-improvement strengthens this supervision on all six evaluated tasks, yielding better retrieval than human calibration on four.
The training value persists at larger scales: on MS MARCO, retrieval gains continue across a 32-fold range of synthetic training-data sizes.
SYNTRA thus enables scalable embedding-model adaptation with minimal human intervention.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
papers.summary:
Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused.
Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response.
Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step in the trajectory, and (2) observation targets, such as web pages and terminal logs, are long and noisy and reach only one step ahead.
We propose CoPE, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets.
On successful on-policy trajectories, CoPE trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences that follows each history.
Each action is also supervised when forecast from the preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that the shared backbone absorbs during training, and this enables acting and forecasting to co-evolve.
The policy still acts one step at a time at inference, with no overhead.
Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, $\tau^2$-bench, and AppWorld), CoPE (1) achieves stronger aggregate performance than GRPO and RL baselines with predictive auxiliary targets across simulated environments, while improving overall performance on both realistic applications; (2) delivers up to $1.9\times$ and $2.0\times$ higher sample efficiency than ECHO and GRPO, respectively, on ScienceWorld; and (3) achieves these gains with a single policy backbone, without additional models, separate pretraining, or inference overhead.
The codebase is available at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/CoPE.
highlights: We propose CoPE, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
papers.summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time.
In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late.
We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference.
Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running.
We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student.
The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted.
Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types.
The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning.
These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.
highlights: outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary:
In LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task.
Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re-executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress.
We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi-agent executions.
Our key intuition is to turn execution-verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives.
First, we collect over 24{,}000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models.
From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs.
It contains 3{,}953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue.
Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS-agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement.
Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run.
The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections.
Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post-hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models.
Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.
highlights: first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: KV-streams for Efficient Compaction in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary:
Scaling the horizon of agentic LLMs is bottlenecked by the need to fit ever longer context traces in GPU memory.
Context compaction has been the most popular mechanism to alleviate this issue, keeping GPU memory constant for a given trace.
Unfortunately, most compaction strategies rely on prefilling the LLM context many times over, hindering training throughput.
To alleviate this bottleneck and enable efficient trainable compaction, we propose KV-streams, a plug-and-play strategy compatible with any compaction strategy that substantially increases throughput while showing no evidence of hindering performance.
KV-streams enable scalable compaction by streaming the KV cache forward rather than flushing it after each compaction.
We show that KV-streams enable three different compaction strategies, achieving a 2.6 to 5x wall-clock speedup in training.
Beyond efficiency, we find that the streamed KV cache can act as a recurrent state, carrying forward information that has long since disappeared from the context.
Specifically, in a controlled setting we show that, contrary to prior work, RL alone is all that is needed for this behavior to emerge.
Overall, we show KV-streams to be an efficient and lightweight plug-and-play addition to any post-training pipeline.
highlights: Scaling the horizon of agentic LLMs is bottlenecked by the need to fit ever longer context traces in GPU memory.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.summary:
Language model agents increasingly automate post-training, but when given the full training stack they converge on supervised fine-tuning and spend most effort revising training data.
Existing systems give the agent one kind of control, selecting rows from a fixed pool or calling a generator, whereas a human data engineer adjusts proportions, prunes, repairs, replaces and synthesizes the data.
We design a data action space for these changes and ask whether an automated system can make the full range rather than one of them, and what structure that requires.
We first run this loop with a single agent, and it reaches only one action, adjusting category proportions, while its context fills with execution output and is discarded mid-search.
We therefore introduce \textbf{AutoSFT}, a multi-agent system where a meta agent separates execution from analysis, gathers proposals from independent angles, and calls a synthesis subagent for capabilities the pool cannot cover, with the model, the trainer, and the budget fixed within each comparison.
Adding each component in turn helps: the executor halves context loss, the analysis subagents lift the best IFEval by $+6.5$, and synthesis adds $+3.4$ IFEval and $+2.9$ IFBench.
The same loop transfers to code, where analysis adds $+3.7$ MBPP+ over a single agent that does not improve.
Every result comes from runs that retrain from the base model each round, so each component's effect is individually attributable.
Our findings suggest that automating SFT data research depends more on covering diverse data actions than on a stronger single action.
highlights: first run this loop with a single agent

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
papers.summary:
As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important.
Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions.
Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks.
We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource.
This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests.
We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent.
These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes foregoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements.
We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings.
Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models.
Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies.
SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.
highlights: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: StepSafe: Learning Timely Intervention with Context-Aware Safety Reasoning
papers.summary:
Safety in agentic systems is inherently sequential: whether an action is safe depends on prior actions, tool outputs, information disclosures, and interactions among agents.
Recent work has shifted agent safety guardrails from post-hoc trajectory-level assessment toward step-level action diagnosis and proactive risk prediction, yet existing training objectives provide limited supervision for how step evidence accumulates over time and when it becomes sufficient to justify intervention.
We propose \methodlong~(ASPO): a training framework for step-level timely intervention.
Pre-fix level stage alignment allows crediting each decision at its own step: it compares each response with the other responses sampled at the same prefix and rewards the action that fits the stage, continuing before the risk is visible, asking while clarification can still avert harm, and stopping before harm is irreversible.
Adaptive feedback self-distillation further credits the reasoning behind each decision, with the model itself as a teacher that sees the step annotations on intervention steps and rules mined from its own false alarms on safe steps.
Its training data carry a violation taxonomy and an intervention window at every step and are extended through self-evolving multi-agent red-teaming.
Finally we present \textsc{StepSafe}, a step-level reasoning guardrail with timely intervention, that achieves the state-of-the-art peformance among open-source guardrails across five agent-safety benchmarks on safety-utility pareto curve with Youden's $J$ of 53.0 (4B) against 46.2.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
papers.summary:
AI agents take actions through tools.
Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably.
Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions.
We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets.
We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity.
In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels.
In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout.
In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises.
We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls.
Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points.
All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels.
Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero.
The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels.
This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance.
The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard.
We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: SSR: Structural Signal Retriever for Scalable Agent Discovery in LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary:
Large-scale multi-agent ecosystems require mechanisms for discovering suitable agents without exposing entire registries to a large language model (LLM) orchestrator.
The challenge is not only to retrieve relevant Agent Cards from a growing registry, but also to maintain a compact candidate context, since each additional candidate increases prompt size, inference cost, latency, and the risk of exceeding the model context window.
We formulate this problem as candidate-context scalability and propose the Structural Signal Retriever (SSR), our deterministic and training-free retrieval method designed for Agent Card discovery.
SSR derives structural lexical signals from capability-bearing Agent Card fields, weights them using inverse document frequency (IDF), and uses an Inverted Signal Index (ISI) for selective candidate scoring.
We evaluate SSR using a synthetic agent benchmark, a public MS MARCO adaptation, and end-to-end LLM orchestration.
At 1,000 agents, SSR reduces LLM input by 98.8% and orchestration latency by 70.9% relative to full-catalog orchestration.
On MS MARCO, IDF improves retrieval effectiveness within the structural representation, while the ISI preserves retrieval effectiveness and reduces explicitly scored passages by 96.8%.
End-to-end experiments show that candidate pre-selection maintains a compact candidate context as registry size grows and avoids the operational failures observed with full-catalog orchestration.
These results support SSR as an Agent-Card-native, traceable retrieval mechanism for candidate-context scalability.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: WorkflowPerturb: Calibrated Stress Tests for Evaluating Multi-Agent Workflow Metrics
papers.summary:
Multi-agent LLM systems that generate structured workflows from natural-language requests are now deployed in production across cloud automation, DevOps, and enterprise orchestration.
Operating them exposes a recurring change-management problem.
Routine updates, such as re-running an input, swapping the LLM, or refactoring an agent's prompt or orchestration code, often produce workflows that differ substantially from validated references.
Engineers then lack a principled way to decide whether a change is safe to ship.
Automatic workflow evaluation is the natural tool, but in practice metric scores are poorly calibrated, and a numeric change rarely communicates the severity of the underlying degradation.
We introduce WorkflowPerturb, a controlled benchmark that applies realistic, graded perturbations to golden workflows.
It contains 4,973 golden workflows and 44,757 perturbed variants across three perturbation types (Missing Steps, Compressed Steps, Description Changes) at severities of 10%, 30%, and 50%.
We benchmark multiple metric families, analyzing their sensitivity and calibration using expected score trajectories and instance-level alert rates.
Our results characterize systematic differences across families and support severity-aware interpretation of workflow evaluation scores in change-management settings.
WorkflowPerturb is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/microsoft/WorkflowPerturb .
highlights: Operating them exposes a recurring change-management problem.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
papers.summary:
Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations.
In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical.
We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal.
We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation.
The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge.
The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance.
With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks.
Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance.
Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific errors rather than to errors in software usage.
CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.
highlights: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying e

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: MasDrift: Benchmarking Authorization Preservation Across Multi-Agent Architectures
papers.summary:
Multi-agent systems (MAS) decompose long-horizon tasks across supervisors and subagents, but delegated goals do not necessarily carry their original authorization boundaries.
Existing safety benchmarks mainly study adversarial compromise, while work on constraint drift lacks controlled architecture-level evaluation.
We introduce MasDrift, a benchmark of 600 benign productivity tasks across eight domains.
Each task pairs required work with reserved actions.
MasDrift compares single-agent, centralized, and decentralized coordination while varying hierarchy depth and peer width, measuring task completion and authorization preservation.
Across generic multi-agent conditions, centralized hierarchies achieve 93.9--98.6% task completion versus 85.7--87.0% for peer networks, while unauthorized actions occur in 2.7--19.8% of tasks versus 0.6--0.8%, a gap that widens with hierarchy depth.
We further compare two defenses that differ in where authorization evidence resides.
One re-anchors every pending call to the original user request.
The other carries an attenuated policy along the delegation chain.
Re-anchoring reduces unauthorized actions in every model configuration we evaluate, at a cost of 1.6 points of pooled completion.
Chain propagation blocks required work instead, forfeiting up to 36.3 points.
A heterogeneous case study confirms that the failure follows from coordination rather than model strength.
MasDrift exposes a centralization tradeoff and makes authorization preservation a measurable property of MAS design.
highlights: Existing safety benchmarks mainly study adversarial compromise, while work on constraint drift lacks controlled architec

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty
papers.summary:
Deep research agents are increasingly deployed to retrieve precise information from large corpora, yet multi-hop, long-horizon tasks remain challenging.
Synthetic data generation has emerged as a scalable solution, with existing pipelines typically expanding seed tasks to increase their apparent depth and breadth.
However, this expansion does not reliably translate into necessary reasoning: newly introduced evidence may be only weakly coupled to the answer, creating a mismatch between intended and empirical difficulty.
To address this problem, we introduce GRADS, a graph-guided agentic data synthesis framework with explicit difficulty control.
GRADS runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question--answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required to derive each answer.
At each step, it conditions generation on a relevant subgraph, preserving indispensable inference without accumulating irrelevant context.
Experiments across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains show that GRADS consistently generates verified tasks with empirically separated difficulty distributions, as measured by independent solvers.
Moreover, under matched training budgets, post-training on this data delivers consistent gains at every level: SFT raises the solution-termination rate to over 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and on our held-out, domain-specific benchmarks, the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet~4 on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains.
highlights: surpasses it on the scientific and security domains

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs
papers.summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly.
Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next.
Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price.
We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success.
To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment.
The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points.
Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it.
Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels.
On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev.
On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success.
The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.
highlights: Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
papers.summary:
As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show.
Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence.
However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis.
To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine.
Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence.
We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed.
Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM.
The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
highlights: outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary:
The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control.
While the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) enables centralized optimization, current AI approaches lack reasoning capabilities and explainability.
We propose eXplainable RIC (X-RIC), a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures.
X-RIC combines reactive Reinforcement Learning (RL) with strategic agentic reasoning through: (i) automated Behavioral Cloning (BC) using domain heuristics for sample-efficient training, (ii) a Telecom Language Model (TLM), a transformer-based reasoning module providing contextual abstraction and interpretability, and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation within the Near-RT RIC control loop enabling continuous policy refinement.
To ensure deployment readiness, we introduce BARX (Benchmarking Agentic Reasoning for RAN), a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic control across latency, compliance, and determinism metrics.
We validate X-RIC on SLA-aware network slicing in simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments.
X-RIC achieves 89% operational cost reduction while maintaining SLA compliance, converging 75% faster with 50% fewer training steps and 46% lower variance.
highlights: The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
papers.summary:
Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions.
For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window.
However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems.
Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM.
Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space.
Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering.
Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents.
Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory.
In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%.
Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.
highlights: For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Agentic Coding
papers.summary:
As coding agents increasingly undertake real-world work autonomously, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted has become important.
Existing work evaluates related agent behaviors from separate perspectives, but lacks a systematic framework for unifying these behaviors.
To bridge this gap, we introduce ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents.
Grounded in the well-established Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework in software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes its 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings and contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence.
We further introduce dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness, using a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation.
Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models and a post-hoc human study reveal that (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, with substantial variation across agent configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, while treatment violations substantially harm developers' experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; and (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings, suggesting that knowledge from human practice can guide the diagnosis and improvement of this capability.
highlights: first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Telling FIBS: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception
papers.summary:
Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people.
We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens.
Our probes surpass black-box monitors on agentic coding benchmarks, achieving 98.3% AUROC in SHADE-Arena and 98.0% in BashArena (vs.
97.7%, 97.6% resp.
for action-only text monitors), and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up.
We further test probes on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone; in these cases of introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or knowledge of a model's training data.
In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model's true hidden goal from other goals with an AUROC of up to 99.7%.
Our probes also detect deception on prominent open-weight models which lie about politically sensitive topics when put under pressure.
We release our training dataset, dubbed FIBS, to help drive frontier deployment of effective probes, and encourage the community to expand upon it with further examples of deception and sabotage.
highlights: surpass black-box monitors on agentic coding benchmarks

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
papers.summary:
Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token.
Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured.
Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint.
Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps.
A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs.
Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept.
Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost.
CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association.
Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged.
Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments.
Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size.
Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix.
The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score.
Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920
highlights: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review
Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics
papers.summary:
Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt.
We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents.
Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all.
Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers.
Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it.
Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss.
Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes.
Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.
highlights: We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: MemComposer: Learning to Assemble Memories for LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary:
Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters.
However, semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness: downstream performance depends on how memories are selected and presented to the agent.
We propose MemComposer, a memory composer that jointly examines the current query and retrieved candidates to decide which experiences to include, how many to select, and how to order them.
We train the composer using Experience Policy Optimization (ExPO), a GRPO-based framework that evaluates assembled memory contexts through complete agent interactions and uses task-success feedback to optimize the assembly policy.
Across three $\tau^2$-bench domains with two frozen executors, MemComposer outperforms the strongest baseline for each executor while reducing average memory-token usage by 16.9% and 4.9%, respectively.
The learned policy also transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and benefits from memories generated by stronger models without further training.
These results demonstrate the value of learning query-specific memory assembly using downstream task feedback.
highlights: outperforms the strongest baseline for each executor while reducing average memory-token usage by 16
Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation
papers.summary:
Multi-agent reasoning with large language models (LLMs) raises a central question for collective decision-making: when agents disagree, whose decision should be trusted?
Resolving such disagreements is difficult because agents' decisions are susceptible to non-semantic biases such as majority pressure and response-style preferences, which can obscure the quality of the underlying reasoning.
Our analysis shows how bias can be both mitigated and exploited: bias control improves initial answer selection, while bias injection elicits decision instability that serves as a reliability signal.
Building on these findings, we introduce a test-time aggregation framework that requires neither validation data nor prior knowledge of relative model strength.
The framework implements bias control by presenting one style-normalized reasoning trace per distinct answer, and bias injection by placing each aggregating agent's initially selected answer in the minority.
Overall, our framework achieves higher average accuracy and better token efficiency than competing non-oracle aggregation methods across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four heterogeneous LLM combinations.
It also improves final-answer accuracy when applied to multi-agent debate and Mixture-of-Agents, without modifying their interaction or synthesis processes.
highlights: Bias Control and Injection for Multi

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Constrained Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Imagination
papers.summary:
Predicting cost in a multi-agent world model moves most constrained policy updates into imagination: the stronger model-free baseline needs $10$ to $20$ times CA-MAMBA's interactions on the median SMAC configuration, and CA-MAMBA earns $2.8$ to $12$ times the baselines' MAMuJoCo reward at equal budget.
In controlled tests on one task per benchmark, pricing the model's cost advantages at parity more than halves a cost-blind learner's cost and meets a tight continuous-control limit the learned multiplier misses, suggesting the model's cost estimates are not the bottleneck.

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Discussions
papers.summary:
LLM systems increasingly rely on groups of agents that discuss, critique, and check one another, assuming that peers will catch individual errors.
We test this assumption against a minimal adversary.
In a ten-agent factual discussion, one or three adversarial agents repeatedly assert a plausible false answer.
After each round we probe each benign agent's private answer through a separate call whose response is hidden from its peers, and we separately label its public stance toward the claim.
Across six models and three factual-QA datasets, groups remain stable without an attacker: only 0.6% of benign agents finish with the false answer.
A single adversarial agent increases this rate to 44.8% and three to 60.5%.
Studies of conformity typically report public agreement without private change; we find the reverse.
With three adversarial agents present, benign agents hold the false answer in 51.6% of exposed turns but publicly endorse it in only 19.7%.
Much of the influence therefore remains invisible in the discussion, and the false answers persist when agents are asked for their own views.
Agents that retain the true answer often fail to defend it; once adopted, the false answer spreads among benign agents, and baseline knowledge does not predict robustness.
highlights: LLM systems increasingly rely on groups of agents that discuss, critique, and check one another, assuming that peers wil

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: RefactorPlatform: An Open-Source Harness for Controlled Evaluation of Repository-Scale Refactoring Agents
papers.summary:
Repository-scale refactoring requires coding agents to propagate a single change across many interdependent files without altering program behavior, yet to our knowledge no existing harness isolates the design choices that determine agent success on this task.
We present RefactorPlatform, an open-source evaluation harness that holds the environment fixed and varies each design axis explicitly: model backbone (via OpenRouter and GitHub Copilot CLI), execution regime (baseline, retrieval-augmented, and multi-agent), and prompt specificity.
Each run executes in an isolated workspace with live terminal streaming, per-task logging of tokens, diffs, and transcripts, AST-based verification, and exportable telemetry for audit and reproduction.
Demonstrating the platform on 100 multi-file RefactorBench tasks across four model families, we illustrate the analyses it supports: AST-aware chunking outperforms naive token-window chunking by 25-30 percentage points (pp) across prompt modes, whereas naive retrieval falls below the retrieval-free baseline; a lean retrieval-augmented single agent (86%) beats the sub-agent configuration we evaluated (66%) on matched tasks with no task passing under delegation that fails under retrieval; and retrieval's accuracy gains absorb its token overhead, leaving cost per successful refactoring unchanged.
RefactorPlatform is open-sourced to make refactoring-agent evaluation reproducible and auditable.
highlights: outperforms naive token-window chunking by 25-30 percentage points (pp) across prompt modes

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent
papers.summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex tasks, including code generation, tool use, and multi-hop question answering.
Existing self-improvement methods enhance agent performance through model optimization, harness evolution, and executable artifact refinement, while recursive self-improvement (RSI) further extends optimization to the improvement mechanisms themselves.
However, adapting self-improvement workflows to evolving performance bottlenecks while improving workflow orchestration through execution feedback remains a key challenge.
We propose \textbf{RSIFlow}, a \textbf{R}ecursive \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{I}mprovement framework that integrates adaptive work\textbf{flow} orchestration with meta-agent capability evolution.
RSIFlow diagnoses performance bottlenecks from task-agent trajectories and environmental feedback to dynamically select component-specific improvement workflows.
The meta-agent then distills workflow outcomes into component-specific skills and cross-component principles, evolving its own harness to improve subsequent workflow orchestration.
Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all benchmarks.
Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of adaptive workflow orchestration and meta-harness evolution.
Code is available at https://github.com/1HUAN1/RSI-Flow.
highlights: Experiments across six benchmarks and two backbone models show that RSIFlow achieves the SOTA average performance on all

papers.groupName: Agent / RSI / Agentic RL 主题
papers.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.summary:
Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions.
As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements.
However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use.

featuredPapers.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
featuredPapers.authors: Yufa Zhou, Yichen Wang, Jiakun Fan
featuredPapers.summary:
Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence.
We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential.
We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs.
We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code.
The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next.
They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models.
Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of.
In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.
To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average.

With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task.

featuredPapers.title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
featuredPapers.authors: Yilong Xu, Minrui Xu, Xinyu Zhou
featuredPapers.summary:
Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context.

featuredPapers.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
featuredPapers.authors: Miao Su, Yucan Guo, Zixuan Li
featuredPapers.summary:

Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries.

Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%.

featuredPapers.authors: Yijia Mao, Song Dai, Tao Chen
featuredPapers.summary:
Can AI agents organize scientific investigations that lead to well-supported conclusions?
To evaluate this capability, we introduce PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring physics areas.
Each task specifies the research objective and essential scientific constraints, while leaving the agent to organize the investigation and determine how to generate and validate the evidence needed to answer the question.
A 20-criterion Atomic Score measures local scientific accomplishment, while Research Closure (RC0--RC4) assesses how fully the investigation resolves the specified research question based on whether its indispensable evidence requirements and applicable scope conditions are satisfied.

Case-level analysis further illustrates how misinterpretation of generated results and unresolved physical applicability limits can lead to incomplete closure.
Together, these results reveal a persistent gap between AI agents' local scientific accomplishments and their ability to achieve complete research closure.

featuredPapers.authors: Yanchen Deng, Jianguo Huang, Yao Long Teng
